parts.partTitle: Maven vs. Gradle: The Build Engine Showdown

beats.headline: Why does your build fail on CI but work locally?
beats.subline: It is not your code; it is your build tool configuration. Let us fix that.
beats.narration: Why does your build fail on CI but work locally? It is usually a mismatch in build tool configuration. You are not just compiling code; you are orchestrating a complex dependency graph.

beats.title: Maven vs. Gradle Paradigms
beats.narration: Maven uses a rigid, declarative lifecycle—compile, test, package. It is predictable and standard. Gradle uses a dynamic task graph, calculating exactly what changed to skip unnecessary work.

beats.title: Maven Lifecycle Internals
beats.subtitle: Phases vs. Plugin Goals
beats.narration: Do not confuse phases with goals. A phase is just a milestone. A goal is the actual plugin logic bound to that phase. Maven runs the chain; you just define the target.

beats.title: Dependency Scopes Explained

steps.explanation: Keeps driver classes off your compile classpath, preventing accidental dependency on database-specific internals.

beats.narration: Use runtime scope for your JDBC drivers. It keeps your business logic clean by preventing direct imports of database-specific classes that should only exist at runtime.

beats.title: Part 1 Summary
takeaways: Use runtime scope for JDBC drivers
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Solving the Dependency Diamond Hell →
beats.narration: That is the foundation. In Part 2, we tackle the diamond dependency problem—why your build picks the wrong version and how to force alignment.

beats.headline: Why is your build downgrading your libraries?
beats.subline: Transitive dependencies are a silent killer. Here is how to control them.
beats.narration: Why is your build silently downgrading your libraries? It is the diamond dependency problem. Two libraries need different versions of the same JAR, and your build tool has to pick a winner.

beats.title: The Diamond Conflict
beats.subtitle: Root -> LibA(v25) & LibB(v32)
beats.narration: Maven picks the version closest to the root. Gradle picks the highest version. Both can cause NoSuchMethodError if the version chosen is missing methods required by your code.

beats.title: Diagnosing the Tree
beats.caption: Stop guessing, start tracing

lines.text: selection reason: forced by highest version

beats.narration: Never guess why a JAR was pulled in. Use dependency tree in Maven or dependencyInsight in Gradle. These commands show you exactly which library brought in that unwanted version.

beats.title: Aligning with BOMs

steps.explanation: Forces all managed dependencies to use the versions defined in the BOM, overriding transitive conflicts.

beats.narration: Use a Bill of Materials, or BOM. It centralizes version alignment. By importing it in dependency management, you force your entire project to use tested, compatible versions regardless of graph depth.

beats.title: Part 2 Summary
takeaways: BOMs are the source of truth for versions
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Compilation Avoidance & API vs Implementation →
beats.narration: Dependency hell is now manageable. In Part 3, we optimize your build speed using Gradle's compilation avoidance and the difference between api and implementation.

beats.headline: Why does your build recompile everything?
beats.subline: You are likely leaking dependencies. Here is how to fix it.
beats.narration: Why does your build recompile everything every single time? You are likely leaking dependencies. If you use the wrong configuration, you force downstream modules to recompile unnecessarily.

beats.title: Compilation Avoidance
beats.subtitle: API vs Implementation
beats.narration: Use implementation by default. It hides the dependency from downstream compile classpaths. Only use api if the dependency types are part of your public method signatures.

beats.title: Configuration Phase Pitfall

steps.explanation: This code runs during every Gradle invocation, even ./gradlew clean, slowing down every single build.
Defer all I/O and network calls to doLast to keep your build cacheable and fast.

beats.narration: Never put network calls or I/O in the configuration block. It runs every time you invoke Gradle, even if you are just cleaning. Defer these to doLast to keep your build cacheable.

beats.title: Build Wrappers
beats.narration: Stop relying on global installs. Use the wrapper. It pins the exact build tool version in Git, ensuring that your local machine and CI runner are always perfectly in sync.

beats.title: Part 3 Summary
beats.narration: Your build is now fast and reproducible. In Part 4, we wrap up with a final checklist and the lab command to master these tools.

beats.headline: Is your build production-ready?
beats.subline: Check these four pillars before you ship.
beats.narration: Is your build actually production-ready? Before you ship, verify these four pillars. If you cannot answer yes to all of them, your build is a technical debt time bomb.

beats.title: The Production Checklist
beats.subtitle: 4 Pillars of a Solid Build
beats.narration: Reproducibility via wrappers, dependency hygiene via BOMs, build speed via caching, and CI integrity by removing all local state. This is the gold standard for Java builds.

beats.title: Final Analysis
beats.caption: Run this before every release
beats.narration: Run dependency analyze in Maven or build scans in Gradle. These tools catch unused dependencies and performance bottlenecks that you would otherwise miss until production crashes.

beats.title: The Golden Rule
beats.narration: Never manage JARs manually. If you are copying files into a lib folder, you have already lost. Let the build tool handle the classpath and artifact lifecycle.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
beats.narration: You have mastered build tools. Checkout the branch to run the lab, and visit the roadmap for the full JavaHub curriculum. Keep building.
